title: Honey: Nature's Wonder Sugar
summary: Chuck and Josh explain what honey is and how bees make it: nectar is carried in the bee's crop, mixed with enzymes and pollen, and dehydrated into honey; honeydew honey is also covered. They discuss the history of beekeeping (about five thousand years, Egypt, Indus Valley, Mesopotamia, China), honeycomb and wax, and the composition of honey (mostly fructose and glucose plus complex sugars, amino acids, enzymes, polyphenols, flavonoids). Health claims are discussed, including allergy relief from local honey, anti-inflammatory effects, Manuka and Tualang honey, wound healing for diabetic foot ulcers, blood pressure, cancer research, and neurological effects, with caveats about the need for more study. The episode covers honey grading: raw, filtered, ultrafiltered, pasteurized, creamed/spun, color grade, organic, monofloral versus multifloral, and flavored honeys. A brief listener mail segment closes the episode.

segments.title: Playlist intro
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Thanksgiving-spring playlist episode on honey and the hosts open the show; Jerry's connection is late.

segments.title: Opening banter and spun honey
segments.summary: Casual banter about eating spun honey on toast, an unrelated song story, and Josh's request for an episode on honey.

segments.title: Beekeeping cross-reference
segments.summary: Chuck notes the earlier beekeeping episode and the bee TV episode, and recommends listening to the beekeeping episode.

segments.title: How bees make nectar into honey
segments.summary: Nectar is carried in the bee's crop, which holds a large amount of nectar, and back to the hive.

segments.title: Regurgitation, enzymes and dehydration
segments.summary: Bees pass nectar mouth to mouth, mix in enzymes, and dehydrate it; pollen can be mixed in; Chuck says it isn't really bee vomit.

segments.title: Honeydew honey
segments.summary: Honey can also be made by bees from honeydew, sap from stems, leaves and bark produced by aphids.

segments.title: Honey bee species
segments.summary: The western honeybee is the main honey producer and was domesticated; the hosts discuss sustainable harvest.

segments.title: History of beekeeping
segments.summary: Honey hunting goes back to the Mesolithic; beekeeping is thought to date back about five thousand years in Egypt, the Indus Valley, Mesopotamia and China, with clay pot hives and the Winnie the Pooh skep image.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Sponsor break.

segments.title: Composition of honey
segments.summary: Honey is mostly simple sugars, fructose and glucose, plus complex sugars, amino acids, enzymes, polyphenols and flavonoids. Honey also has acidity and antibacterial properties and can be reliquefied if it crystallizes.

segments.title: Heating honey and animal testing
segments.summary: Discussion of whether heated honey becomes toxic, with few studies found; Chuck comments on animal restraint-stress research in mice.

segments.title: Off-topic banter
segments.summary: Hosts chat about tomorrow cocktails, Montenegro, and a Los Angeles dinner.

segments.title: Honey and allergies, health and inflammation
segments.summary: Studies found local honey reduced allergy symptoms, with the claim that local honey exposes people to local pollen. Flavonoids may reduce inflammation by blocking inflammatory protein expression.

segments.title: Manuka and Tualang honey
segments.summary: Manuka honey, a monofloral honey from New Zealand, is popular and expensive; it has methylglyoxal as its active antimicrobial compound. Tualang (jungle) honey from Malaysia is rising as an alternative.

segments.title: Topical honey and wound healing
segments.summary: Honey applied to wounds, especially diabetic foot ulcers, is discussed; Chuck notes manuka's potency may hinder healing.

segments.title: Blood pressure and study limitations
segments.summary: Some studies found honey reduced hypertension in women but not men; the hosts stress that honey studies are inconsistent.

segments.title: Honey and cancer
segments.summary: Lab and clinical results suggest honey can induce apoptosis and blebbing in cancer cells.

segments.title: Neurological effects and daily dose
segments.summary: A study on seniors with a daily tablespoon of honey showed lower dementia rates than placebo; the hosts advise replacing added sugar with honey rather than adding it.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Second break.

segments.title: Honeycomb and beeswax
segments.summary: Honeycomb is the hexagonal wax structure; beekeepers provide wax foundation, saving bees about six pounds of honey per pound of wax.

segments.title: Raw, strained and pasteurized honey
segments.summary: Honey sold in the US is usually strained; raw honey is a misnomer for unpasteurized honey. Pasteurization is rarely needed and is mainly for smoothness.

segments.title: Filtered, ultrafiltered and diatomaceous earth
segments.summary: Filtered honey has finer filtering; ultrafiltered honey is warmed and diluted and the USDA says it can't be called honey; diatomaceous earth can be used to filter honey.

segments.title: Creamed honey and honey color grades
segments.summary: Creamed or spun honey is the same as regular honey; honey is graded on a Pfund color scale from water white to dark amber.

segments.title: Organic honey
segments.summary: Organic honey is a separate classification that can apply to any processing style if organic methods are used.

segments.title: Monofloral versus multifloral and flavored honeys
segments.summary: Monofloral honey comes from one flower; multifloral honey from many. Flavor notes such as citrus, linden, eucalyptus, and buckwheat are described, along with flavored honey varieties.

segments.title: Celebrity honey and honey compound properties
segments.summary: Flamingo Estate's celebrity-branded honey for charity is mentioned; Chuck lists the many properties attributed to compounds found in honey.
